Team Perihelion is participating virtually in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our objective is to develop a practical, well-researched solution using NASA’s open data.

Skills sought: software developers (Python or JavaScript), data analysts or researchers, and a designer or communicator to prepare the presentation and demonstration.
summary:
**OUTPOST ZERO** is an interactive lunar mission survival simulator designed to train young astronauts in the challenges of living and working on the Moon. Players take on the role of a mission commander responsible for keeping a lunar crew alive through a simulated 30-day mission. They must manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, energy, and building materials while constructing and maintaining life-support systems, preparing for extreme lunar nights, and protecting the crew from radiation and equipment failures.

The project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by turning complex space-exploration concepts into an engaging, hands-on learning experience. Through realistic resource-management decisions, mission predictions, interactive habitat visualizations, and post-mission analysis, players discover how one system affects another and why careful planning is essential for survival in space.

OUTPOST ZERO makes space science more accessible to students while encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and an understanding of the engineering challenges behind future human missions to the Moon.
details:
Project Details – OUTPOST ZERO

OUTPOST ZERO is an interactive lunar mission survival simulator developed to help students understand the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human presence on the Moon. It places players in the role of a mission commander responsible for keeping a crew alive during a simulated 30-day lunar mission.

How does it work?

Players manage a lunar habitat by balancing essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, energy, and construction materials. They can build and upgrade systems, including solar panels, batteries, oxygen generators, CO₂ scrubbers, water recyclers, greenhouses, and radiation shielding. Each decision affects the habitat's other systems and the crew's survival.

The simulation introduces challenges such as the extreme lunar day-night cycle, solar storms, radiation exposure, equipment failures, and limited resources. Players must predict upcoming risks, prioritize power distribution, maintain equipment, and make strategic decisions. At the end of the mission, they receive a performance report explaining their decisions, resource usage, survival outcomes, and the causes behind critical events.

Benefits and intended impact

The project transforms complex space-exploration concepts into an interactive learning experience. Instead of simply reading about life-support systems, students experience how these systems depend on one another. It encourages critical thinking, resource management, problem-solving, scientific curiosity, and an understanding of the engineering challenges involved in future lunar exploration.

Our intended impact is to make space science more accessible and engaging for younger learners while inspiring interest in STEM education and human space exploration.

Tools and technologies used

  • HTML – Structure of the application.
  • CSS – Interface design, layout, animations, and visual presentation.
  • JavaScript – Game logic, resource management, mission simulation, random events, and interactive features.
  • SVG – Visual representation of the lunar habitat, its modules, and system connections.
  • Web Audio API – Generated sound effects and audio feedback.
  • Node.js testing tools – Testing simulation logic and checking game behavior.
  • Git and GitHub – Source-code management and project collaboration.

The project is designed to run directly in a web browser without requiring complex installation or additional frameworks.

What makes the project creative?

Our main creative approach is combining a survival strategy game with a simplified scientific simulation. Players do not just collect resources; they must understand the relationships between systems. For example, insufficient battery capacity during the lunar night can interrupt oxygen generation, while a failure in the CO₂ scrubber can affect crew health.

The project also includes an AI-style mission assistant named Pip, mission predictions, interactive system-flow visualizations, and a feature that compares different survival strategies using the same mission conditions. These features help players understand not only what happened but also why it happened.

Factors considered during development

Our team considered scientific relevance, educational value, accessibility for younger students, gameplay balance, and the interconnected nature of lunar life-support systems. We also considered the Moon's long day-night cycle, radiation hazards, limited resources, equipment reliability, and the importance of redundancy in critical systems.

Our goal was to create more than a conventional space-themed game: we wanted to build an educational mission simulator that helps players appreciate the planning, engineering, and decision-making required to sustain human life beyond Earth.
